Synthesis of vinylidenecyclopropanes via gold(I)-
catalyzed cyclopropanation of vinyl arenes with
c-stannylated propargyl esters †
Hiroto Mori, a Yusuke Ono, a Shota Nakagawa, a Sota Akima, a Miki Murakami, b
Toshinobu Korenaga,
 *cd Tadashi Nakaji-Hirabayashi,
 be Mayumi Kyogoku b and
Yoshikazu Horino
 *a
The reaction of c-stannylated propargyl esters in the presence of a
cationic gold( I) catalyst aﬀords vinylidenecyclopropane derivatives
as a mixture of diastereomers. The cis-geometry of the alkenes is
almost entirely retained in the product. DFT calculations suggest
the involvement of the gold( I)-stabilized propargyl cation as a
resonance form of gold( I)-coordinated allenylidene species.
Cyclopropanes are important functional molecules found in
numerous natural products,1 bioactive molecules,2 and ligands
in catalysis,3 and are a platform for further transformations. 4 In
particular, vinylidenecyclopropanes (VDCPs) are synthetically
valuable molecules
5 owing to their remarkable properties com-
pared to other simple cyclopropanes and alkylidenecyclopro-
panes, including an inherently higher strain energy than simple
cyclopropanes
6 as well as a synthetically versatile allene moiety.7
VDCPs are typically synthesized by the [2+1] cycloaddition of
carbenes with unsaturated compounds (Scheme 1a). 8 However,
the synthetic utility of this method is limited by its requirement
for a strong base and the additional steps to prepare 1,2,3-
butatrienes.
9 Another approach to the synthesis of VDCPs
involves the Pd(0) 10- or Cu( I)11-mediated substitutions of 1-
alkynylcyclopropyl chlorides; however, the synthesis of 1-
alkynylcyclopropyl chlorides requires multiple steps. In con-
trast, transition metal allenylidene species are suﬃciently
stable for use in organic synthesis and are readily generated
by alkyne activation.
12 The cyclopropanationo fa l k e n e st h r o u g h
transition-metalallenylidene species is therefore a straightforward
approach to the synthesis of VDCPs. Transition metal allenylidene
complexes typically react via a similar mechanism to that of
transition metal vinylidene complexes; thus, nucleophilic addi-
tions can occur at both the a-a n d g-positions of the allenylidene
complex depending on the nature of the metal and the nucleo-
phile. Although several allenylidene-mediated C–C bond forming
reactions at the g-position have been devised using various
transition metals, including Cu and Ru, studies investigating
the reactivity of the a-position of transition metal allenylidene
species have lagged significantly behind.
13 Buono’s seminal work
on the [2+1] cycloaddition of strained alkenes with palladium
allenylidene species is the only example of a catalytic C–C bond-
forming reaction at the a-position (Scheme 1b).
14 Gold catalysis
has recently emerged as a powerful tool for three-membered ring-
forming reactions;
15 thus, we hypothesized that as yet unexplored
gold(I)-coordinated allenylidene species will provide a novel route

to the catalytic synthesis of VDCPs.Despite considerable progress
in the development of gold-catalyzed alkene cyclopropanation
reactions,16 alkene cyclopropanation for the synthesis of VDCPs
via ag o l d (I)-coordinated allenylidene s p e c i e si su n d e r d e v e l o p e d
owing to a lack of synthetic methods that afford such intermedi-
ates. Since the pioneering stu dy on the preparation of a gold( I)
(alkoxy)(amino)allenylidene complex by the Hashmi group, 17 Ber-
trand synthesized gold(I) mono- and bis-allenylidene complexes
derived from a cyclic (alkyl)(amino)carbene (Fig. 1).18 Later, Wide-
nhoefer first synthesized and structurally characterized gold( I)
diarylallenylidene complexes lacking heteroatom stabilization.19
Despite these seminal studies, only stoichiometric carbon–
heteroatom-bond-forming reactions have been achieved.
19 The
exploration of catalytic C–C bond forming reactions via ag o l d (I)-
coordinated allenylidene speciesor its resonance form, the gold(I)-
stabilized propargyl cation, has therefore emerged at the forefront
of current research.
20 We herein report the synthesis of VDCPsvia
the gold(I)-catalyzed cyclopropanation of vinyl arenes (Scheme 1c).
The reaction conditions were optimized based on the reac-
tion of 1a and styrene ( 2a). In the presence of (Ph 3P)AuCl/
AgSbF6 (5 mol%) in CH 2Cl2 (0.2 M) at 25 1C, the reaction
aﬀorded the desired VDCP 3aa in 57% yield as a 2 : 1 mixture
of diastereomers (Table 1, entry 1). Reducing the amount of 2a
diminished the yield of 3aa (entry 2). Screening of the counter
ion, ligand, and gold complex 21 showed that the combination
of (Ph 3P)AuCl and AgSbF 6 exhibited high catalytic activity to
give 3aa (entries 1 and 3–6). The choice of ligand did not
significantly influence the diastereoselectivity of the reaction.
However, prolonging the reaction time led to decreased diaster-
eoselectivity and partial decomposition of 3aa, indicating that
the gold(
I)-mediated isomerization of 3aa is involved (entry 7).22
In addition, CH 2Cl2 was the optimal solvent. 23 Finally, 3aa was
obtained in 68% yield by reducing the concentration (entry 8).
No reaction occurred in the absence of (Ph 3P)AuCl (entry 9).
The scope of the reaction was examined under the optimal
conditions using various vinyl arenes (Scheme 2). The gold( I)-
catalyzed cyclopropanation reaction of halogenated styrenes 2b
and 2c with a chloro or bromo group at the para position gave
3ab and 3ac in 52% and 40% yields, respectively. The cyclopro-
panation reaction is sensitive to the electronic eﬀects of the
substituents on the phenyl ring of styrene. For example, although
p-MeO- and p-CF
3-substituted styrenes were not compatible, the
cyclopropanation of o-vinylnaphthalene and o-triisopropylsilyl
(TIPS)-ethynylated styrene proceeded to aﬀord 3af and 3ag in
43% and 56% yields, respectively. In addition, the chemoselective
reaction of the styrene double bond ofo-(3-butenyl)styrene yielded
3ah in 57% yield. Furthermore, the present method was also
applicable for a-substituted styrenes, such as a-methyl, a-phenyl,
and a-cyclopropylstyrenes, aﬀording3ai–ak in moderate to good
yields. Interestingly, cyclopropanation of cis-stilbene did not
proceed under the optimized conditions; however, trans-stilbene
afforded the desired product3al in 44% yield. Similarly, cyclopro-
panes 3am and 3an were obtained from the cyclic alkenes such as
indene and 1,2-dihydronaphthal ene. The applicability of the
reaction conditions at larger scales was demonstrated by the
synthesis of 3am in 80% yield. In all cases, VDCPs were obtained
as a mixture of diastereomers. In contrast, although aliphatic
alkenes and benzofuran are known to participate in the gold( I)
carbene-mediated alkene cyclopropanation,16,23 performing the
reaction using them failed in the present system.
We also examined the substrate scope to assess the influ-
ence of the electronic nature of the propargyl substituent on the

reaction (Scheme 3). Phenyl groups at the propargylic position
bearing bromo ( 2b and 2c), trifluoromethyl ( 2d), phenyl ( 2e),
trimethylsilyl (2f), and methyl ( 2g–i) groups at the ortho-, meta-,
and para-positions yielded the corresponding VDCPs 3ba–ia
in low to good yields. The major isomer of 3hc was determined
to be syn.23 The cyclopropanation reaction was found to be
sensitive to the presence of oxygen-containing functional
groups. For instance, the 3,5-dimethoxyphenyl-substituted sub-
strate 1j exhibited significantly lower reactivity than substrates
without oxygen-containing groups, yielding only trace amount
of the desired product 3ja. The reaction conditions also toler-
ated unsaturated substituents, including o-allyl, o-homoallyl,
and o-(TIPS)-ethynyl groups, to afford 3ka–ma, and alkene and
alkyne remained intact. Although the desired product 3nc
could not be obtained using 1,1-dimethyl-3-(tributylstannyl)-
propargyl acetate, changing from an acetoxy group to a pivaloyl
group furnished 3nc in 28% yield.
To investigate the stereochemical course, we next achieved
the reaction of 1n with the cis- and trans-b-monodeuteri-
ostyrene derivatives cis-2c-d and trans-2c-d (Scheme 4a and b).
23
The reaction was stereospecific with respect to the alkene configu-
ration. For example, the reaction of1n with cis-2c-d proceeded with
complete retention of the double bond configuration. Similarly, the
alkene geometry of trans-2c-d was also retained completely in the
product. In addition,cis-a n dtrans-2c-d were recovered without any
isomerization after the reaction with 1n. Moreover, a control
experiment was conducted to clarify the mechanism. Gold(
I)-
catalyzed reaction of 1a (91% ee) with 2c furnished 3ac in 40%
yield with complete loss of enantiomeric excess (Scheme 4c).
Furthermore, reaction of1o, which possesses a SiMe
3 group instead
of SnBu3, yielded a complex mixture (Scheme 4d).
A tentative reaction mechanism based on the above results
and our previous study24 is presented in Scheme 5. The complexa-
tion of 1 with the gold( I) complex generates the vinyl cation
intermediate A, which is eﬃciently stabilized by complexation,
hyperconjugation with theb-stannyl substituent, and conventional
neighboring group participation of the acetoxy group. p-
backdonation from gold(I) induces rearrangement of the stannyl
group to aﬀord the gold( I) carbene intermediate B,w h i c hw o u l d
then produce the gold(I)-coordinated allenylidene speciesC via a
bimolecularanti-specific elimination.25 DFT calculations were per-
formed to obtain further details on the cyclopropanation
mechanism.
23 Although the cyclopropanation of styrene with
gold(I)-coordinated benzylidene species has been proposed to occur
via a concerted mechanism, 26 our calculations show that the
cyclopropane ring is constructed by a stepwise mechanism. The
vinyl arene 2 attacks the Ca carbon of the gold( I)-stabilized pro-
pargyl cation species D as shown in E to give the carbenium
intermediateFa (1st step). Electrophilic cleavage of the [Au] + via
the interaction of the back lobe of the Au–C a bond with the

benzylic cation affords3 (2nd step).26 The activation free energies of
both steps indicated that the 1st step is slower than the 2nd step. In
addition, although there is a possibility of equilibrium betweenFa
and Fb, higher activation free energies than the energies of the 2nd
step make this equilibrium impossible.23 Therefore, the reaction
proceeds straightforwardly without branching along the way, which
is consistent with the experimentally observed stereochemical out-
come, as shown in Scheme 4a and b.
In conclusion, we have developed a mild and general
method for the synthesis of VDCPs via the gold(
I)-catalyzed
cyclopropanation of vinyl arenes. This method represents the
first catalytic method for the synthesis of VDCPs via the
cyclopropanation of vinyl arenes. Further exploration of new
methodology via a gold(
I)-stabilized propargyl cation species is
currently underway in our laboratory.
